beats.narration_text: Someone assumed Claude would track their legal deadlines — watch the case, notice the rule, sound the alarm. That's not what this skill does. It's arithmetic: you hand it a triggering date and the rule that governs it, and it computes the resulting date. Here's what actually happens when you run it.

beats.narration_text: Start with the anatomy. A skill is a folder Claude reads before it works — this one is called deadlines, and it contains one file, SKILL.md. That file is the whole program, written in plain English. No hidden logic, no compiled binary, no black box. The design choice: legibility over cleverness. You can open the instructions and audit every step Claude will take.

props.title: A skill is a folder.
props.calloutText: The SKILL.md is the instruction set.

beats.narration_text: The pipeline sits in the Steps section. Claude reads each step in order and runs it — top to bottom, no branching unless a step explicitly asks for one. They optimized for predictability at the expense of flexibility: same input, same order, same output, every time. Which is exactly what you want when the output is a legal date.

Here's the interesting constraint. Give it a triggering date — the event that starts the clock — and the rule that governs it: a filing window, a response period, a statute of limitations. It computes the resulting date. That's the whole mechanism. Stay inside that rule and the calendar is exact every time. Feed it the wrong rule and it will confidently return the wrong date. The skill computes; it does not decide which rule applies.

beats.narration_text: Same rule in, same calendar out, every time — that's the whole promise. What it doesn't do: figure out which rule actually governs your matter. That part is still yours.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Give it a triggering date and the rule that governs it, then ask it to walk you through the calendar arithmetic step by step: identify the trigger event, apply the rule, flag any weekend or holiday shifts, and return both the raw computed date and the effective due date. Before it computes anything, have it tell you exactly what it needs from you to be sure the answer is right. Go deeper: change one variable and re-run the calculation. What if the triggering date lands on a Friday? What if the rule counts business days instead of calendar days? Watch which shifts change the outcome and which don't — that's how you find out where the rule is actually load-bearing.
